steps.en: What you see: A dropout in the interventricular septum carries colour flow across it from left to right. Small restrictive defects show a high velocity jet above 4 m per s. The left atrium and left ventricle dilate with volume overload in moderate defects. Large non restrictive defects flatten the septum as pressures equalise across it.

Normal values with units: Restrictive jet velocity. Peak velocity around 4 m per s or more implies a left to right gradient near 64 mmHg by four times velocity squared, marking a restrictive defect.. Source: ASE 2019 transthoracic examination guideline, section on Doppler and haemodynamics

Left ventricular cavity. Normal diastolic diameter about 42 to 58 mm in men and 38 to 52 mm in women. Above this with a defect means volume overload.. Source: ASE 2015 chamber quantification guideline, section on left ventricular size

Pulmonary pressure from tricuspid jet. Tricuspid velocity above 2.8 m per s suggests raised pulmonary pressure and needs a full right heart study.. Source: ASE and EACVI 2016 diastolic function guideline, section on tricuspid regurgitant velocity

ECG and heart sound correlation ecg: Small restrictive defects show left ventricular hypertrophy. Large defects show biventricular hypertrophy. Right ventricular hypertrophy warns of pulmonary vascular disease.

ECG and heart sound correlation sounds: A harsh pansystolic murmur at the left lower sternal edge marks the shunt with a palpable thrill in moderate defects. A single loud second sound warns of pulmonary hypertension.

What to report: Defect position and size with the views that show it
Jet direction and peak velocity with the implied gradient
Left heart chamber sizes for volume overload
Pulmonary pressure estimate and any aortic cusp prolapse or regurgitation
Red flags needing urgent referral: Cyanosis with shunt reversal, needs urgent paediatric cardiology review for Eisenmenger physiology
Heart failure in infancy with a large defect, needs urgent surgical review
New aortic regurgitation with a membranous defect, needs urgent review for cusp prolapse
Pitfalls: Infected vegetations settle on defect rims, so look for mobile masses in any febrile patient.
Multiple muscular defects hide behind one jet, so sweep the whole septum in two planes.
Pulmonary vascular disease silences the murmur while the defect persists, so never use the murmur to rule out.
Figure: Short axis at aortic level shows the basal septum only. Sweep serial short axis levels plus apical views to find muscular defects. View tte_psax_av

todo.en: How to get it on the probe, step by step: Start in the parasternal long axis to see the basal and membranous septum with colour on. Then assess the mid and apical septum in short axis and apical four chamber and two chamber views.
Drop the colour scale to catch low velocity flow in large defects.
Record continuous wave Doppler through the jet and note the peak velocity.
Measure left atrial and left ventricular size for volume overload.
Estimate pulmonary pressure from any tricuspid regurgitation jet.

Common mistakes and how to correct them: Calling septal dropout near the aortic valve a defect. Fix: Lower colour gain and confirm the jet in two planes. True defects persist, dropout vanishes with a small angle change.
Missing a large low gradient defect with a high colour scale. Fix: Reduce the colour scale and sweep slowly. High scale settings hide low velocity shunts.
Missing aortic cusp prolapse into a membranous defect. Fix: Check the aortic cusps in long axis. A prolapsing cusp can close the defect and mask its size.

q.en: Which finding marks a small restrictive defect?

o.en: High velocity left to right jet with normal chamber sizes
Low velocity bidirectional flow with equal pressures
No flow with a dilated right ventricle

why.en: A small hole keeps a large pressure difference, giving a high velocity jet with normal chamber sizes.

q.en: A child with a known defect turns blue on crying. What next?

why.en: Cyanosis suggests shunt reversal with pulmonary vascular disease, an urgent paediatric cardiology problem.

q.en: Which valve can prolapse into a membranous defect?

why.en: A cusp of the aortic valve can prolapse into a membranous defect and cause aortic regurgitation.
